utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are we ready for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President. We hope you've recovered from the flu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When we broke last Friday, we had a witness who was testifying in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go back to the closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While we are preparing, Mr. President, I'm told that, and they were already given to the Defence, but I'd like to distribute binders to the Chamber, to the Judges, if they have not already been, a binder of exhibits that will be used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please get the binders as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I did overhear the request of the interpreters, Mr. President, and I understand that there are binders for the interpreters as well, so... Mr. President, the testimony of this witness will go to primarily Background, paragraphs 10 and 11; General Allegations, paragraphs 18 to 21; paragraphs -- excuse me, count 1, paragraphs 27 and 34; and count 18, paragraphs 53 and 54. And as I mentioned, he will be testifying in -- with no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good evening. Good evening, Sir Martin. I apologise for keeping you waiting. We have a few minutes to go this evening, we can at least begin the introduction of your testimony this evening. Sir, is it correct that you are a retired general officer of the Royal British Marines?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes. I served for 37 years in the Royal Marines. My last three years were as commandant general of the Royal Marines in the rank of Lieutenant General.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And sir, just so the Judges will understand that position, is it accurate to say that the commandant general of the Royal British Marines is the senior officer, that is, the overall senior officer in charge of the entire British marine force?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you retired in approximately 1990, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes, I retired in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think it goes without saying, Sir Martin, and I will not go through all the details of your military career, but in your 37 years you served in a number of positions and ranks and in a number of locations?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I would like to do, sir, if I could, is direct your attention now to the time following your retirement from the Royal Marines. Did you -- and I'm going to go through this somewhat quickly and then go back to the most pertinent time period for the purposes of your testimony here, but is it correct, sir, that at about -- at the end of June, 1993, you were sent on a mission by the European Community Monitoring Mission, otherwise known as ECMM, as an official in the Mostar office of that mission?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes. I volunteered to serve with the EC Monitor Mission and I went out to Bosnia and I was posted to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I would -- I should warn you and myself - I've already been cautioned - that because you and I both speak English, we tend to respond to each other, question and answer, quite quickly, which makes it quite difficult for translation, so both of us will have to try to make a bit of a pause. Thank you. Now, sir, when you -- your first position in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the ECMM, that was as the head or the chief person in charge of the coordinating centre for Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm going to come -- I'm going to come in a few minutes to give you the opportunity to tell us more about the ECMM and the way it was organised but first through your various positions. And you continued in that position, sir, from about June, 1993 or very late June, 1993, to approximately April, 1994, that is with ECMM?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes, I spent three months in Mostar and then, in October, I was sent up to Zenica, to central Bosnia, to take charge of all the ECMM operations in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And that location or that part of ECMM was known as RC - in other words, regional centre - Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you maintained -- or excuse me, you remained in that position until about April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I'm correct, sir, then you served in the European Union administration in Mostar from approximately April of 1994 to July, 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes. The first few months was the advance party period, then the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 8327 to 8336. actual administration, EU administration of Mostar started properly with the inauguration of Hans Koschnik from Germany as the administrator in July, 1996, for a two-year mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during that time, in relation to Mr. Koschnik, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: I was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to characterise that position as the number 2 position, then, in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Well, technically, the number 2 was -- well, in fact, the number 2 was the diplomatic adviser, Mr. Klaus Mescher [phoen] of Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: So I suppose I was the third in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you continued in that position until July 1996, and then from July, 1996, to December of that year, did you serve as the European Union special envoy in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes. Because the elections which were due to take place at the end of the EU administration had been delayed, it was running behind time, and the EU decided that it would be necessary to have a further six-month period to stabilise the situation in Mostar and so the office of the EU special envoy was established, and I was appointed the EU special envoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I will again remind the Chamber, if it may assist, that I will come back to some of these matters in more detail in the body of Sir Martin's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that then following that position, from approximately January, 1997, to October, 1998, you were the senior representative of the office of the high representative, that position being for all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but you being his representative in the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: That is correct. It was decided on the end of the EU to establish a regional office of the high representative based in Mostar but covering the southern third of Bosnia from Trebinje in Republika Srpska to Dvar in the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally in this regard, after some break in service, did you, from July 1999 to November 1999, serve as a UN regional administrator in the town of Mitrovica in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I understand that resume correctly, then, sir, is it fair to say that you had a number of senior positions, either directly in or closely connected to Mostar, from approximately the end of June, 1993, until approximately October of 1998?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from my six months in Zenica in central Bosnia, I was in Mostar for five and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And even when you were in Zenica, sir, as I understand it -- I'm sorry for the speed -- your authority or jurisdiction, if you will, continued to extend over the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: That is correct. My area covered from Tuzla in the north to Mostar in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, backing up specifically to your appointment, your first appointment as head of the coordination centre in Mostar, who did you follow in that position?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: My immediate predecessor was a German, Klaus Nissen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then when you moved on to take command or control of the regional centre Zenica, who took over as the head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: On a temporary basis, it was my deputy down there, who was Spanish, Jesus Amatriain, and then I sent down from Zenica a man called Philip Watkins to take over as head of CC Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where had Mr. Watkins previously been assigned?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: He'd spent, I think it was about nine months in central Bosnia in the Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you took the position of the head of RC Zenica, who did you follow in that position?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: I followed a French diplomat, Jean-Pierre Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during the time during the approximate three-month period that you were the head of the Mostar CC, was -- in terms of the organisational structure of ECMM, was Mr. Thebault your superior or the person you reported to?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes. He was my direct superior as the head of the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, a little bit about ECMM. Can you just describe to the Chamber - and they've certainly heard a bit about ECMM in the course of the trial, but can you tell them a bit more about the mission of ECMM and the mandate that it had in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I will try and keep it as short as possible. The ECMM was established initially to monitor the ceasefire in Slovenia and then its role was expanded into Croatia and then on to Bosnia and so on. It was intended to be part of the whole -- another instrument towards working towards peace in the whole region, and it was divided into seven regional centres. There was the headquarters of the whole ECMM in Zagreb the Hotel E, then the seven regional centres: There were two in Croatia, Zagreb and Knin; one in Bosnia, Zenica; then there was Szeged, Sofia, Tirana and Belgrade. Now, those regional centres had under them coordinating centres. So if we take the example of Bosnia, there was the regional centre in Zenica, and three coordinating centres; Tuzla, Travnik and Mostar. Each coordinating centre had a number of monitor teams under it. For example, in Mostar, I had four teams. Mike 1 in Jablanica, Konjic to the north; Mike 2, Mostar; Mike 3, Medjugorje; and Mike 4, to the west in Tomislavgrad. Each team consisted of four members; two international monitors of different nationalities, one driver and one interpreter. We were all dressed in white, distinctive white; white flak jackets, white helmets when necessary, and we travelled in white cars, white vehicles. The fundamental role was report -- although we did a lot of negotiating, discussing, go-between between the various parties and so on, the fundamental role was reporting, reporting in the following order: Political matters, military matters, and then humanitarian matters. At the end of each day, each team would send in a written report to the coordinating centre. The coordinating centre would amalgamate a report and dispatch it to the regional centre, and all the regional centres would send in combined reports to the main headquarters in Zagreb, and from then on, they would produce a comprehensive report which would go to the EU presidency and all the nations who are involved in the actual ECMM, so that first thing in the morning, they had a full, comprehensive report of what was going on throughout the whole of the former Yugoslavia, which was right up to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Thank you very much. I might direct -- if the witness could be shown the bundle or the binder of exhibits prepared for him, and if I can direct the courtroom's attention to the first exhibit in that bundle, in the very just few minutes we have remaining, I could ask you to look, please, at Exhibit P86.1.

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've done such a thorough job in the last few minutes that you've covered most of what's in this document, but nonetheless, it might assist the Chamber in the future. Can you just briefly cast your eyes on that document and tell the Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: This is a summary of the agreement in Brioni on the 7th of July, 1991, which was established -- when the ECMM was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And this, is it correct, talks about the basic -- it starts out with talking about the role, talks about the main mode of action, as indicated here, and a bit about the organisational structure as you've told us in the last few minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me pick up on a point -- few points of clarification. I'm sorry, I'm once again picking up too much speed. It is probably known, sir, to most people in the courtroom, perhaps everyone, but so the record is clear, a few moments ago, you were referring to the teams as Mike 1, Mike 2, et cetera, and I assume -- is it correct that you're using Mike as a military reference to the initial M?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, yes, that's the M for -- because it was Mostar, Mike, absolutely right. I should have explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in addition to another -- other few details before we conclude this evening, you mentioned that all the ECMM monitors were dressed in white. Is it also correct that they were at all times unarmed?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Always unarmed, but nearly always travelling in armoured [Realtime transcript read in error "armed"] Mercedes, four-wheel-drive vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this indicates --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, on the transcript, it seems to have come across as "armed" Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I assume, Sir Martin, the Mercedes were not armed, but did you mean to say they were armoured?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Armoured, armoured, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And in connection with the seven regional centres you mentioned, and concluding RC Zenica, is it correct, then, that RC Zenica, with one or two exceptions which you can explain to us, was essentially then the headquarters ECMM office for the vast majority of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Martin Garrod
utterances.text: Yes. From Zenica, all the ECMM operations were covered, but we did not have monitors in Republika Srpska, nor did we have monitors in the Bosniak pockets -- wrong -- yes, Bihac, Zepa, Gorazde and Srebrenica, nor in Sarajevo. So it was basically the central area of Bosnia which was in due course to become the basis of the federation between the Bosniaks and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would submit that might be an appropriate moment to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sir, as I did with other witnesses, during your stay here in The Hague, please do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we will resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of January, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
